title: Assessing team leadership and management choices
blurb: Judge whether a project manager's choices build an effective team: closing skill gaps, building social cohesion and leading across organizations.
question: A project team is split between Edinburgh and Pune. To save travel costs, the project manager cancels a planned week in which the Pune leads would plan wave 1 alongside the Edinburgh team. Is this appropriate, and why?

teach.body: A project team is temporary, cross-functional and often spread across organizations and places. Its leader may have less formal authority than a line manager, and some team members may be more senior than the project manager. So PRINCE2 expects the project manager to lead through collaboration, build the team on purpose, close skill gaps and create social cohesion, especially when people are not in one place.

rows.label: What it is
values: Instructing tasks in agreed ways of working

teach.caption: Both are needed. Leadership is what makes people willing to work within the agreed ways.

teach.body: Match a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives to the project's needs. People with the same skills perform a role differently, and the same person performs differently with different colleagues, so roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, seen through key relationships. Generic, standard role descriptions are unlikely to work. Understand competencies, find the gaps and mitigate them, for example by upskilling or shifting tasks to more suitable people.

steps.label: Understand
steps.sub: Competencies and capabilities of each person

steps.label: Mitigate
steps.sub: Upskill, or shift tasks to more suitable people

teach.caption: A qualification is not proof of competence: experience and skill in the task are what count.

teach.body: Make good use of people's time and build social cohesion: people meeting purposefully and regularly, building trust across project silos. Co-located teams share information naturally through formal and informal networks. Virtual, remote or hybrid teams need deliberate methods, for example synchronized co-location days for key people, focused on key relationships. Structured team-building exercises can speed up team formation, and safety and well-being matter throughout.

rows.label: Good method
values: Synced co-location days for key people

teach.body: Many people the project depends on sit outside its direct authority: supplier staff, other departments, people who will integrate the products into their work. Leading them needs cultural intelligence, the ability to relate and work across the cultures within the organizational ecosystem. Co-creating work and ways of working with them, rather than issuing orders, makes people more willing to work in line with what has been agreed.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Brennan Mutual, Project Skyline (S6)
items: The society's IT staff have few cloud skills and the cloud partner's engineers are split between Edinburgh and Pune, across two time zones.
Mairi Campbell (PM) maps each person's skills against the landing zone and migration work, then pairs society engineers with partner engineers for the pilot wave: closing gaps by upskilling.
She schedules a planning week each quarter when Arjun Menon and his Pune leads work alongside the Edinburgh team: deliberate cohesion for a distributed team.
She notices Pune engineers rarely challenge plans in meetings led from Edinburgh, so she agrees with Arjun how concerns will be raised: cultural intelligence across organizations.

teach.text: Watch for options that turn a people action into a different practice: using a cohesion event to collect progress is the PROGRESS practice; asking the executive to impose authority on people outside their line rarely works. And 'a PRINCE2 qualification closes the gap' is false: competence comes from skill and experience in the task.

items: Leadership persuades, influences and co-creates; management instructs tasks within agreed ways of working.
Build teams from diverse capabilities; roles reflect capability, authority and availability; avoid generic role descriptions.
Find competency gaps and mitigate them by upskilling or shifting responsibilities.
Distributed teams need deliberate social cohesion, such as synchronized co-location days for key people.
Lead across boundaries with cultural intelligence and co-creation, not orders.

summary: You can now judge whether a project manager's team choices are appropriate: building a team from diverse capabilities, closing competency gaps, creating social cohesion for distributed teams and leading across organizational boundaries. You can also reject options that confuse these with progress reporting or formal authority.

A.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, few of the society's engineers have cloud skills. In the foundations stage, quality reviews find repeated errors in the network security set-up done by a society engineer who has never worked on cloud. What should the project manager do NEXT?
options: Ask the senior supplier to write a fuller role description for the engineer
Pair him with a partner engineer and move the security work until he is ready
Keep him on the task, since people with the same role perform it differently
Raise an exception report, as the quality tolerance for the stage may be breached
A.why: Competency and capability gaps should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities to more suitable people (3.3.2). Pairing does both.

whyNot.0: A better role description does not give him the skills; generic descriptions are themselves a weakness.
whyNot.2: That statement is true, but it does not justify leaving a known gap in place on security work.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests a forecast breach of stage tolerance; this is a people problem the project manager can fix.

A.q: At Wenmoor Community Health most project team members work part-time on rotas across three localities and can usually join meetings online at lunchtime. They barely know each other and work in locality silos. The project manager arranges a monthly in-person half-day for key members from all three localities, focused on how the triage hub and locality teams will work together. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because distributed teams need deliberate ways to build trust across silos
Yes, because the half-days let the PM gather progress for the highlight reports
No, because team members will share information naturally as the project runs
No, because the half-days use clinical time that would need to be backfilled
A.why: Virtual, remote or hybrid teams need social cohesion to be built deliberately, for example through synchronized co-location days for key people focused on key relationships (3.3.3).

whyNot.1: Gathering progress is the progress practice; the purpose here is cohesion and trust between localities.
whyNot.2: Natural information sharing happens in co-located teams; this team is spread across localities and rotas.
whyNot.3: People's time should be used well, but a monthly half-day for key people is a proportionate way to build cohesion.

A.q: On Calderbrook's permit project the supplier's delivery manager, who will act as team manager, has far more digital delivery experience than the council's project manager. Before the first work package is authorized, the project manager works through it with him, agreeing the products, tolerances and reporting arrangements together. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because co-creating the work package suits a team leader who is senior
Yes, because the team manager sets the tolerances for each work package
No, because the executive should authorize work packages to give them weight
No, because a supplier using Scrum should not be given a work package
A.why: The project manager co-creates and reviews the work package with the team manager before authorizing it (16.4.1). It is not unusual for team members to be more senior than the PM, so collaboration rather than instruction is the right style (3.3).

whyNot.1: The project manager sets work package tolerances; the team manager sets tolerances for team members.
whyNot.2: Authorizing work packages is the project manager's job in controlling a stage, not the executive's.
whyNot.3: Work packages are used whatever delivery method the team uses.

B.q: On Carrowford's half marathon, staff from the race company, the council's events team and the volunteer coordinators work in different buildings and rarely meet. The project manager starts a monthly breakfast for them, deliberately with no agenda or status updates, so people from the three organizations get to know each other. How well does this apply the guidance on leading successful teams, and why?
options: It applies it poorly, because each breakfast should be used to collect progress
It applies it well, because purposeful, regular meetings build trust across silos
It applies it well, because structured exercises at the start speed up team forming
It applies it poorly, because not every member will be able to attend each time
B.why: Social cohesion is built by people meeting purposefully and regularly, building trust across project silos (3.3.3). The breakfast does exactly that.

whyNot.0: Collecting progress is the progress practice and would defeat the purpose of the event.
whyNot.2: Structured team-building exercises are a different technique; this is an ongoing regular meeting, not a one-off exercise.
whyNot.3: Attendance will vary, but that does not stop regular contact from building trust.

B.q: At Wenmoor Community Health the project manager is a quality improvement specialist who is new to PRINCE2 7. The executive sees that her first stage plan has no tolerances or product descriptions. He arranges PRINCE2 7 training for her and asks an experienced programme manager from another directorate to mentor her through the stage. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because a PRINCE2 qualification will make her a competent project manager
Yes, because a competency gap should be found and closed, for example by upskilling
No, because the executive should take over the planning until she is trained
No, because the role should go to someone who already holds a PRINCE2 certificate
B.why: Understanding the competencies of people assigned to the project and mitigating gaps, for example by upskilling, is part of building effective teams (3.3.2). Training plus mentoring is upskilling.

whyNot.0: A qualification alone does not guarantee competence; the mentoring is what builds practical skill.
whyNot.2: The executive cannot take on project manager work; that combination breaks a role rule.
whyNot.3: A certificate does not prove competence either; closing this person's gap is a sound mitigation.

B.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit, the project manager notices that engineers in Pune rarely raise problems in meetings led from Edinburgh. She learns this reflects a different working culture around challenging senior people, so she agrees with the Pune delivery lead how his engineers' concerns will be gathered and raised. Which part of leading successful teams is being applied, and why?
options: Social cohesion, because regular purposeful meetings build trust between sites
Closing a competency gap, because tasks move to people better able to do them
Co-creation, because users help design the products they will adopt
Cultural intelligence, because the PM works across cultures in the ecosystem
B.why: Leading people beyond the project's direct authority, often across organizational boundaries, needs cultural intelligence: the ability to relate and work across cultures in the organizational ecosystem (3.3.1).

whyNot.0: No new meeting is set up; the action responds to a cultural difference in how people raise concerns.
whyNot.1: No skill gap is being closed and no tasks are moving between people.
whyNot.2: Co-creation of products involves users and key influencers; the action is about how engineers raise concerns.

C.q: At Tarnside College the project manager gives every team member a role description copied from the college's standard template for that job title, without looking at each person's capability, authority or availability. She says people in the same role all work the same way. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because standard templates save time and keep role descriptions consistent
Yes, because role descriptions belong to the PMT structure set up in starting up
No, because roles should fit each person's capability, authority and availability
No, because each team member should write their own role description instead
C.why: People with the same capabilities perform a role differently, so roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, and generic standard role descriptions are unlikely to be effective (3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Consistency has value, but generic descriptions that ignore the person are unlikely to work.
whyNot.1: Role descriptions are prepared when the project management team is appointed, but that does not justify generic ones.
whyNot.3: Role descriptions are agreed with people, not written by each person alone; the problem is that they were not tailored.

C.q: On Brennan Mutual's data centre exit the team works across Edinburgh and Pune. To protect the cost tolerance, the project manager cancels the planned week in which the Pune delivery lead and two of his team leads would plan wave 1 alongside the Edinburgh team; all planning will now be done by video. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because video meetings let information flow as it would in one office
Yes, because protecting the cost tolerance comes before team-building events
No, because the Pune leads must attend every planning meeting in person
No, because distributed teams need deliberate contact between key people
C.why: For distributed teams, social cohesion must be built deliberately, for example through synchronized co-location days for key people with a focus on key relationships (3.3.3). Wave 1 planning is a key moment.

whyNot.0: Information is shared naturally in co-located teams; a team split across time zones needs deliberate methods.
whyNot.1: Cost matters, but a short planning week for key people is a proportionate cost and nothing suggests a forecast breach.
whyNot.2: There is no rule that every meeting is in person; the point is planned contact for key people at key moments.

C.q: On Carrowford's half marathon the project manager wrote a volunteer briefing procedure herself, and the volunteer coordinators who run the council's volunteering programme have not been following parts of it. She now invites them to redesign the procedure with her. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because co-creating ways of working makes people more willing to follow them
Yes, because the volunteer coordinators should approve all project procedures
No, because the project manager is responsible for writing the project's procedures
No, because management means instructing tasks in line with agreed ways of working
C.why: Co-creation involves the people who will use a product or way of working in designing it, so it is adopted; co-created ways of working make people more willing to be managed in line with them (3.3).

whyNot.1: Approval of project procedures is not the coordinators' role; the point is to design the procedure with them.
whyNot.2: The PM leads, but writing procedures alone has already led to non-compliance; co-creation is the better route.
whyNot.3: That is the definition of management, but these ways of working were never agreed with the people using them.

reteach.title: Equip, connect, lead
reteach.question: For any team question, ask three things: are people equipped, are they connected, and are they being led or merely ordered?

blocks.body: Equipped: does each person have the skills the work needs, and if not, is the gap being closed by upskilling or by moving the task? Connected: do people who must work together actually know and trust each other, with deliberate contact if they are spread out? Led: is the project manager persuading and co-creating, especially with senior or external people, rather than borrowing someone else's authority?

blocks.text: If the option's reason is about reports, tolerances or authority from above, check whether it really explains a PEOPLE action. Usually it does not.

explain.body: Management instructs tasks in line with agreed ways of working. Leadership motivates by persuading, influencing and co-creating through key relationships, and seeks regular feedback.

rows.label: Example
values: Agree how panel rounds fit cycles

test.q: At Fernhollow Foods the new project manager needs the chefs to fit their consumer panel rounds into two-week cycles. She meets the head of product development, explains the launch-week constraint and agrees with her how the panel rounds will fit the cycles. Which statement best describes what the project manager is doing?
options: Managing, because she is instructing tasks in line with agreed ways of working
Leading, because she is persuading and co-creating through a key relationship
Managing, because she is setting tolerances for the team manager's work
Leading, because she is using structured exercises to speed up team forming
test.why: Leadership motivates people by persuading, influencing and co-creating, with a focus on key relationships (3.3). The way of working is being agreed, not instructed.

whyNot.0: Nothing is being instructed; the way of working is being agreed with the head of product development.
whyNot.2: No tolerances are set in this conversation.
whyNot.3: A conversation to agree ways of working is not a structured team-building exercise.

explain.body: Understand the competencies and capabilities of people assigned to the project, identify gaps and mitigate them, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities to more suitable people.

explain.h: Two ways to close a gap

test.q: At Tarnside College nobody in the estates team has commissioned an air-source heat pump system, yet the head of estates will look after the building once it opens. The project manager arranges for him to shadow the contractor's commissioning engineers and adds operator training to the contract. Which statement explains why this is appropriate?
options: Social cohesion is built when people meet purposefully and regularly across silos
Co-creating products with users improves adoption and reduces handover risk
Roles should reflect each person's authority, which the head of estates already has
Competency gaps should be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling
test.why: It is important to understand people's competencies and capabilities, identify gaps and mitigate them, for example by upskilling (3.3.2). Shadowing and training close the gap.

whyNot.0: Shadowing does bring people together, but its purpose here is to build a missing skill.
whyNot.1: Co-creation is about designing products with users; this is training for a skill he lacks.
whyNot.2: His authority is not in question; the gap is in his skills.

explain.body: When teams are virtual, remote or hybrid, cohesion does not happen by itself. Synchronized co-location days for key people, focused on key relationships, are a typical method.

test.q: On Calderbrook's permit project the supplier's Scrum team works in its own offices while the council's staff are at the town hall. The project manager arranges for the council's key staff to spend sprint review and planning day with the supplier's team every two weeks. Which statement explains why this is appropriate?
options: Teams in different places need deliberate methods to build social cohesion
A team in one place shares information through formal and informal networks
Work packages are co-created with the team manager before they are authorized
Highlight reports give the board regular information on the stage's progress
test.why: For teams that are not co-located, cohesion must be built deliberately, for example through synchronized co-location days for key people (3.3.3).

whyNot.1: That describes co-located teams; these teams are in different places.
whyNot.2: Work packages are co-created, but the action here is about regular shared days, not authorizing work.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports are a progress product for the board; this action is about the team.

explain.body: A new project team does not gel by itself. Structured team-building exercises can accelerate team formation, and the project board and project manager also look after the team's safety and well-being.

test.q: On Carrowford's half marathon the race company's operations team, the council's events staff and the volunteer team leaders have never worked together. In the first week of the planning stage the project manager runs a structured half-day exercise in which mixed groups plan the response to a mock race-day incident. Which statement explains why this is appropriate?
options: Lessons from the race company's earlier event are being shared with the team
Tolerances are being tested so that the team knows when to escalate
Structured exercises can speed up the forming of a new project team
Stakeholders who are not in the team are being identified and engaged
test.why: Structured team-building exercises can accelerate team formation for a newly assembled, cross-organization team (3.3.2).

whyNot.0: The exercise may draw on experience, but its purpose is to build a team that has never worked together.
whyNot.1: No tolerances are set or tested; this is a team-building exercise.
whyNot.3: Everyone in the exercise is part of the project team; stakeholder engagement is a different activity.
